newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada likely to beat 1997-98 budget goal-Chretien.
newsitem.headline: Canada likely to beat 1997-98 budget goal-Chretien.

text.p: Canada will most likely do better than its budget deficit targets for the current fiscal year and the next fiscal year, Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Thursday.
He said the government would meet "or even we will do better" than the target of having a deficit equal to three percent of gross domestic product for the 1996-97 fiscal year ending on March 31.
"At the rate things are going, we are very likely to beat our target of two percent for 1997-98," he said in a speech to a business group.
He said more precise information on the 1996-97 deficit would be made available in the budget that Finance Minister Paul Martin was scheduled to release next Tuesday afternoon.
Chretien did not mention when Canada would reach a balanced budget, but indicated Tuesday's budget would allow for some spending increases as the deficit improved.
"We will not budge on our fiscal discipline...not when we are so close," he said. "It will be just plain wrong to step back into an era of high deficits."
Yet he added: "But in our coming budget, as we see the light at the end of the tunnel, we can begin to make wise investments for the future."
He cited as an example measures in the coming budget to try to counter child poverty.
He said the government chose child poverty as the first focus for spending the so-called fiscal dividend -- the result of belt-tightening.
Chretien also said that "in the days and weeks ahead" the government would have specific initiatives to announce in reaction to recommendations from a panel he asked to advise him on health matters.
He gave no details, but key recommendations were to add home care and drugs to Canada's publicly funded health care system.

In a sign of his fiscal optimism, Chretien said: "Forecasters in the private sector are predicting that 1997 and 1998 will be years of strong growth. They say we will lead most of the industrialized world in economic growth.
"They say the economy will create an additional 300,000 jobs a year for the next two years -- on top of the more than 700,000 created since we formed the government."
A finance spokesman for the opposition Reform Party, Monte Solberg, dismissed Chretien's remarks as pre-electioneering. Chretien is expected to call an election this year.
